feed.rights: Explanations and summaries are generated by AI from the original text. Dates, rates and amounts are checked against the source, but errors are still possible, so always rely on the original. Nothing here is legal, tax or investment advice.

entry.title: Faster Key Generation and UC Security Without Global Abort for Lindell's Two-Party ECDSA
entry.summary: Improving Lindell's Two-Party ECDSA: Faster Key Generation and UC Security Without Global Abort IACR ePrint · Nov 25, 2026This paper improves the two-party ECDSA signing protocol by Lindell (CRYPTO '17), addressing its slow key generation and its reliance on a global abort mechanism. The authors build a faster zero-knowledge proof for the Paillier-EC discrete logarithm relation using Bulletproofs and a commitment bridge linking Paillier ciphertexts to elliptic-curve Pedersen commitments. They claim UC security against malicious adversaries without global abort, with key generation time estimated to be about four times faster and small signing overhead. ★★★★ Notable: The authors use Bulletproofs-based commitment bridges to speed up PDL proofs and remove global abort for UC security. They report production implementation performance, relevant to blockchain two-part

entry.title: Proving Security for Paillier-Based VOLE with Reusable Keys
entry.summary: De-Folklorizing Paillier-Based VOLE: UC Security and Reusable Keys IACR ePrint · Nov 25, 2026This paper studies Vector Oblivious Linear Evaluation (VOLE), a basic building block for secure computation, which Paillier-based constructions in threshold ECDSA have used without standalone security proofs. The authors present a two-message Paillier-based VOLE protocol and prove its security in the UC framework under standard cryptographic assumptions. The protocol separates initialization from repeatable execution, so one Paillier key can be reused across many executions and clients, and a server with M clients keeps only one persistent key state.

entry.title: Multi-party approval of maintenance prescriptions on a permissioned blockchain
entry.summary: Multi-Party Authorization of Maintenance Prescriptions on a Permissioned Blockchain arXiv · Nov 26, 2026This paper examines how several organizations can jointly verify where industrial maintenance prescriptions come from and how they were calculated. The authors require endorsers on a permissioned blockchain to check a succinct proof that the agreed model and decision rule produced a prescription before a work order is released. On a four-organization Hyperledger Fabric testbed using a public engine benchmark, this approach stopped all nine contested or mis-operated prescriptions, while hash checks alone accepted four of them.

entry.title: Northstar: Efficient verifiable polynomial arithmetic for encrypted multi-asset tokens and verifiable FHE
entry.summary: Northstar: Efficient Verifiable Negacyclic Polynomial Arithmetic with Applications to Encrypted Lattice-based Multi-Asset ERC-20 and Verifiable FHE arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper presents Northstar, a technique for efficiently proving negacyclic polynomial arithmetic, which is used in lattice-based cryptography to verify that computations were performed correctly. When combined with existing STARK proving frameworks, Northstar achieves better prover time, verifier time, and proof size than prior approaches to verifiable fully homomorphic encryption. The authors also use Northstar to build the first verifiable encrypted multi-asset ERC-20 variant supporting about 1000 assets, which a smart contract can verify efficiently and which they say is practically deployable on current blockchains.

entry.title: Testing Quantum-Resistant and Hybrid Signatures for Blockchains: Speed, Storage and Ledger Size
entry.summary: Evaluating Post-Quantum and Hybrid Signatures for Blockchains: Performance, Storage and Ledger Growth arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper empirically evaluates 13 signature configurations in a common simulated blockchain framework, including ECDSA, ML-DSA, Falcon, SLH-DSA, and hybrids pairing ECDSA with each post-quantum scheme. It measures signing and verification costs, transaction throughput, and signature and public-key sizes, then projects these overheads onto five public blockchains. Falcon-512 verifies nearly as fast as ECDSA, but storage overheads are substantial, with ledger sizes estimated to be 79 to 229 percent larger under the paper's modelling assumptions.

entry.title: Neon-HTLC: Collateral-free hash time-locked contracts with logarithmic timeouts
entry.summary: Neon-HTLC: Collateral-Free HTLCs with Logarithmic Timeout IACR ePrint · Nov 24, 2026This paper addresses the vulnerability of hashed time-lock contracts (HTLCs) to bribery attacks, where miners can be incentivized to censor honest transactions. It shows that existing incentive-compatible HTLCs must trade off between collateral and timeout, and proves this tradeoff holds for a generalized class called two-phase HTLCs, along with identifying optimal parameters. The authors propose Neon-HTLC, which removes the need for collateral by using a punishment that grows exponentially over time, so the timeout scales only logarithmically with payment amount. In their evaluation, a $100,000 payment is secured in 26 blocks with zero collateral, compared with 496 blocks and $5,000 collateral for He-HTLC. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors propose collateral-free, incentive-compatible HTLCs with logarithmic timeout, prove a tradeoff bound for two-phase HTLCs, and report comparisons with He-HTLC.

entry.title: How Many Keys a Quantum Computer Must Break to Control a Proof-of-Stake Blockchain
entry.summary: How Many Keys Must a Quantum Computer Break to Take Over a Blockchain? A Quantum Nakamoto Coefficient for Fifteen Proof-of-Stake Networks arXiv · Nov 25, 2026The paper measures how many validator keys a quantum computer would need to break to take over the voting in fifteen proof-of-stake blockchains, defining a "quantum Nakamoto coefficient." Using live data collected on 15 November 2026, it reports the key counts needed to defeat security guarantees and gain full control. It also derives a formula showing how a 2025 Ethereum change that merged deposits into fewer keys sharply reduced the number of keys required. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a quantum Nakamoto coefficient, derive two formulas, and report checking them on live data from fifteen proof-of-stake networks.

entry.title: Combining blockchain and IoT to manage location and time-stamped data, with its open challenges
entry.summary: Blockchain-IoT Convergence for Spatiotemporal Data Systems: Challenges, Solutions, and Research Gaps arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper examines how blockchain and Internet of Things (IoT) indexing can be combined to improve the management of spatiotemporal data, meaning data tied to both location and time, especially its indexing and querying. It reviews and compares existing literature solutions to highlight challenges. It offers insights for future blockchain-integrated IoT systems in resilient spatiotemporal data ecosystems.

entry.title: AgentBank: A blockchain banking layer for AI agent payments
entry.summary: AgentBank: Banking on Blockchain Agentic Payments arXiv · Nov 24, 2026AI agents pay for data and computation via protocols such as x402 and AP2, but per-agent wallets sit idle and need asset transfers for each payment. This paper presents AgentBank, a smart-contract banking layer that lets agents spend bank liabilities under owner-issued mandates and on-chain spending limits, with internal payments updating balances without transferring assets. Experiments show it cuts idle liquidity by 52-77% compared with per-agent wallets and lowers gas costs for batched internal payments.

entry.title: Pearl: TEE-enabled fair transaction ordering with fewer replicas
entry.summary: Pearl: TEE-Enabled Fair Ordering with Minimal Replication arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper studies fair transaction ordering in blockchain consensus and how trusted execution environments (TEEs) can reduce the number of replicas needed. It proves that, in partially synchronous networks, ordering linearizability and γ-batch-order fairness cannot be achieved with 2f+1 replicas even when TEEs are used, because Byzantine replicas can manipulate submission timing. Under a synchronous network assumption, the authors propose two mechanisms that guarantee these properties with fewer replicas. They integrate these mechanisms into a synchronous lane-based consensus algorithm that outperforms representative baselines while using fewer replicas. ★★★★ Notable: The authors combine TEEs with fair ordering, prove an impossibility for 2f+1 replicas and two synchronous constructions, integrating them into a consensus protocol.

entry.title: PLATRS: A Lattice-Based Linkable Ring Signature for Permissioned Blockchains
entry.summary: PLATRS: A Lattice-Based Linkable Accountable Ring Signature for Permissioned Blockchains arXiv · Nov 23, 2026This paper proposes PLATRS, a module-lattice linkable accountable ring signature scheme for permissioned blockchains, enabling anonymous endorsements that a regulator can open when authorization is reused. The authors prove anonymity, linkability, authority-only traceability, and unforgeability in the random oracle model under M-LWE and M-SIS assumptions. An open-source implementation reports a 107.3 KiB signature at ring size 1024 and throughput measurements on Hyperledger Fabric. ★★★★ Notable: The authors integrate post-quantum security, signer-chosen rings, public event tags and single-authority opening in one lattice scheme, with reported implementation results.

entry.title: Who Makes the Decision? Auditing an LLM Pipeline for Crypto Monitoring
entry.summary: Who Makes the Decision? Auditing an Agentic LLM Pipeline for Illicit Cryptocurrency Transaction Monitoring arXiv · Nov 23, 2026This paper audits an agentic pipeline that monitors illicit cryptocurrency flows using graph detectors, deterministic rules, retrieval-augmented generation, and an LLM judge. Using the Elliptic++ Bitcoin dataset, the authors apply decision-source attribution to determine which components drive flagging decisions. They find that a deterministic wallet-score override accounts for about 94% of the credit for flags, and that the LLM judge tends to follow an injected risk score and cites regulatory clauses that do not apply. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose decision-source attribution auditing and report, on Elliptic++, that a deterministic override carries most flag credit and the LLM judge follows injected scores.

entry.title: A stablecoin whose supply is adjusted by a predictive PID controller
entry.summary: Design an Algorithmic Stablecoin based on a Predictive PID Controller arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper proposes an algorithmic stablecoin controlled solely by a predictive PID controller. Part of the controller's input is a price forecast produced by an ARIMA model. Simulation experiments show that under ideal market conditions, the stablecoin keeps its long-term goals fluctuating within a predefined range. It also consistently returns prices to the anchor interval when exogenous disturbances occur.

entry.title: Paper: Who sent the funds, or how did they move? Auditing sender shortcuts in crypto anti-money-laundering benchmarks on Elliptic2 and Elliptic++
entry.summary: Who Sent It or How It Moved? Sender Shortcuts in Cryptocurrency Anti-Money-Laundering Benchmarks, Audited on Elliptic2 and Elliptic++ arXiv · Nov 23, 2026This paper examines whether graph-based anti-money-laundering models trained on two Bitcoin benchmarks, Elliptic/Elliptic++ and Elliptic2, learn how funds move or only identify the sender. It proposes a diagnostic protocol including a sender lookup baseline and a sender-disjoint split. The authors find that on Elliptic2 the task largely reduces to classifying the sender, while on Elliptic++ this shortcut is negligible, so the diagnostic must be run on each benchmark.

entry.title: "Don't Train It, Write It": An AI Agent Adds New Abilities to a Language Model's Weights
entry.summary: Don't Train It, Write It: An AI Agent Writes New Capabilities into Language Model Weights arXiv · Nov 21, 2026The paper shows an AI agent can add new abilities to a pretrained language model by inserting gated attention heads and MLP neurons into its existing layers, without backpropagation or fitting weights to task answers, using a budget of 50 model passes. Composing modules for six BIG-Bench Hard subtasks raised the normalized BBH score of Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct from 19.95 to 41.05 and Gemma-3-1B-it from 10.25 to 32.86. The authors also report side effects and sessions that failed to produce a module.

entry.title: Reimbursement as a revenue tool in costly clock auctions
entry.summary: Reimbursement as a Revenue Instrument in Costly Clock Auctions arXiv · Nov 21, 2026This paper studies ascending auctions in which bidders incur a cost each time they choose to continue, such as when bidding requires a blockchain transaction. It examines whether a seller can raise net revenue by reimbursing these costs and how reimbursements should be spread across auction rounds. In a two-bidder example, reimbursing only the last scheduled decision yields the highest net revenue among the schedules analyzed. In a four-bidder example, partial reimbursement in earlier rounds earns more than reimbursing only the final decision.

entry.title: Correctable Enrollment and One-Transaction Seed Proofs for Ethereum's Post-Quantum Transition
entry.summary: Correctable Enrollment and One-Transaction Seed Proofs for Ethereum's Post-Quantum Migration arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper proposes a migration design for Ethereum to post-quantum cryptography. Owners can cheaply enroll post-quantum keys using their existing signatures before ECDSA is scheduled for retirement, and can correct the enrollment with a zero-knowledge proof of their BIP-39 seed until a common deadline. Unenrolled accounts stay frozen and can be recovered by seed proof without a deadline. The authors prove account guarantees, model-check the rules, implement the design in go-ethereum and a Lean consensus client, and report a proof of about 190 KB that verifies in 38 ms. ★★★★ Notable: The authors combine correctable enrollment with deadline-free seed proofs for Ethereum's post-quantum migration. They report a go-ethereum implementation and a 190 KB, 38 ms verifying STARK.

entry.title: Modeling joint crypto tail risk and dependence with a copula-based semiparametric framework
entry.summary: Modeling Joint Tail Risk and Dependence for Cryptocurrencies via a Copula-Based Semiparametric Framework arXiv · Nov 21, 2026This paper proposes a Bayesian copula-based bivariate semiparametric framework that jointly forecasts Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall while modeling tail dependence across assets. Marginal dynamics use four ES-CAViaR-type models, and Clayton and BB1 copulas capture dependence. Using Bitcoin and Ethereum data from 2020 to 2025, one-step-ahead rolling-window forecasts are compared with Bayesian DCC-GARCH benchmarks. The framework shows competitive forecasting performance, and lower-tail dependence exceeds upper-tail dependence for most of the period.

entry.title: Freeze Priority Trade-offs in Stablecoin Revocation
entry.summary: Authority Without Priority: The Revocation Trilemma and the Price of Stablecoin Freezes IACR ePrint · Nov 21, 2026Stablecoin issuers can freeze addresses, but a freeze is ordered by block producers like any other transaction, so a later transfer can still execute first. The paper defines revocation priority and proves that, with revenue-maximizing block producers, it cannot coexist with immediacy and neutrality. Using USDT and USDC freezes on Ethereum from 2017 to 2026, the authors study how issuers and targets compete for execution order, and model this competition as a Tullock contest.

entry.title: Pethoa: Dynamic Asset Proofs for Hidden Addresses on Account-Based Blockchains
entry.summary: Pethoa: Dynamic Proofs of Assets for Hidden Address Sets on Account-Based Blockchains IACR ePrint · Nov 22, 2026This paper proposes Dynamic Private Proof of Assets (DPoA), a framework for efficiently updating proofs of assets over hidden sets of on-chain addresses. It splits proof generation into an expensive initialization phase and lightweight per-epoch updates, with zero-knowledge proofs showing each update is correct. The experiments report that a static proof for thousands of addresses takes several minutes on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU, while a dynamic update needs only seconds per block and runs on a 14-core CPU.

entry.title: PCC: Proof-Carrying Credentials for Anonymous, Post-Quantum Delegation
entry.summary: PCC: Proof-Carrying Credentials for Enhanced Anonymity and Post-Quantum Delegation IACR ePrint · Nov 23, 2026This paper proposes PCC, a framework for delegatable anonymous credentials that replaces the explicit delegation chain with a single recursively updated proof-carrying state. Presentation cost no longer grows with delegation depth, and the delegation topology stays hidden from the holder's counterparties. The authors also give a post-quantum-compatible instantiation, and report constant proof size and verification time across tested depths on consumer hardware.

entry.title: TreeOnion: Efficient Private Retrieval of Tree Paths
entry.summary: TreeOnion: Efficient Private Retrieval of Tree Paths IACR ePrint · Nov 21, 2026This paper presents TreeOnion, a single-server scheme that lets clients privately retrieve a root-to-leaf path of nodes from a public database organized as a tree, without revealing which nodes were fetched. For small node sizes, its communication and computation costs are comparable to privately retrieving a single node from the same database. The authors report that TreeOnion is strictly better than alternative approaches in both communication and computation, and at least an order of magnitude better in one of the two.

entry.title: PCC: Proof-Carrying Credentials for Anonymous, Post-Quantum Delegation
entry.summary: PCC: Proof-Carrying Credentials for Enhanced Anonymity and Post-Quantum Delegation arXiv · Nov 20, 2026This paper proposes Proof-Carrying Credentials (PCC), a framework for delegatable anonymous credentials that replaces the explicit delegation chain with a recursively updated proof state, so presentation cost does not grow with delegation depth. It formalizes Enhanced Delegation Anonymity (EDA), which combines verifier-side anonymity with holder-side topology hiding. The authors also give a post-quantum-compatible instantiation in the QROM using transparent FRI-based recursion and hash-based signatures.

entry.title: Bottlenecked: Capital Cost of Protected DeFi Lending
entry.summary: Bottlenecked: The Capital Cost of Protected DeFi Lending arXiv · Nov 20, 2026This paper studies how to allocate junior capital that absorbs losses before users in DeFi lending protocols suffer them. It models user assets, covered liabilities, and junior capital as a tripartite graph and defines an adversarial default premium (ADP) to measure the cost of this protection. The authors find that designs resembling Aave and Morpho have insurance costs scaling as Θ(N), while optimized graphs can reduce this to Θ(√N), with estimated savings of up to 34.5% on 2026 attack cases.

entry.title: Intergalactic Consensus: Asynchronous Bitcoin Clients, a paper on how Bitcoin clients can confirm blocks safely when message delivery is not timed
entry.summary: Intergalactic Consensus: Asynchronous Bitcoin Clients IACR ePrint · Nov 16, 2026The paper notes that existing Bitcoin clients assume messages arrive on time and at least one peer is honest. It proposes a client that needs neither assumption, relying only on a local clock and confirming blocks based on the current round and the height of the chain it receives. Under the bitcoin backbone model, the authors prove the rule is safe and live. They also analyze the latency cost of asynchrony, showing that such a client discards a portion of honest chains and confirms blocks Θ(r) rounds later than synchronous validators, a bound they show is tight. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose an asynchronous Bitcoin client confirmation rule, prove safety and liveness, and report a tight latency lower bound.

entry.title: Cleve's Bound Is Tight: Optimal Fair Coin Flipping for Fixed Party Counts
entry.summary: Cleve's Bound Is Tight: Optimally Fair Coin Flipping for Every Fixed Number of Parties IACR ePrint · Nov 17, 2026This paper studies fair multi-party coin flipping, where colluding parties can bias the result by aborting when there is no honest majority. The authors present an r-round protocol for n parties whose bias against n-1 corrupted parties is O(n^3 2^n / r), under assumptions of constant-round oblivious transfer and passively secure computation.
